First birthdays

Smash Cakes: What to Order for a First Birthday

A smash cake is a small cake made to be handled and demolished by the birthday child. What it is, how makers build it, and how to order one alongside the main cake.

You have seen the photo. A one year old sitting in front of a small cake, both hands buried in buttercream, icing in the hair, a look of complete concentration on their face. It has become one of the most photographed moments of an Australian first birthday, and it has a cake of its own.

A smash cake is a small cake made to be handled and demolished by the birthday child, usually while someone is taking photos. It is almost always ordered alongside the cake the guests eat, not instead of it. This guide covers what a smash cake actually is, how makers build them, the ideas that photograph well, and how to brief one in with the rest of your kids birthday cakes order.

The basics

What a smash cake is, and what it is not

A smash cake is a single small cake, usually one tier and single serve, made for one person to pull apart. It is not designed to be cut, served or shared.

Its whole job is to survive being picked up, squashed and sat in for a few minutes while the camera is going.

That is a very different brief from the main celebration cake. The main cake has to serve a room, hold its shape on a table for a few hours and look right in the background of every photo. The smash cake only has to look good for one short stretch and then come apart easily in small hands.

Most families order both. The smash cake comes out for the photos, often before or after the formal candle moment, and the larger cake is cut and served to the guests. Some parents keep the two moments separate so the smash happens outside or on a drop sheet, which saves a great deal of cleaning up later.

Ordering both from the same maker also means the two cakes relate to each other instead of clashing, which matters when they end up side by side in the photos.

How it is made

Size, shape and how it is built

Smash cakes are small and low for practical reasons. A one year old needs to be able to reach into the top of it while seated, so a tall cake is the wrong shape entirely.

Most makers work to a compact round, somewhere in the range of a small single tier, with enough height to look like a proper cake in a photo and not so much that it topples when it is pushed.

What gets left out matters as much as what goes in. Dowels, internal supports, wires, toothpicks, plastic picks, hard figurines and anything sharp or rigid are normally kept out of a smash cake altogether, because the cake is built to come apart under hands. Decorations tend to be made from the same soft materials as the cake covering so that the whole thing behaves the same way when it is pushed.

The covering choice shapes the moment too. A soft buttercream finish gives way immediately and makes the mess everyone is hoping for. Firmer coverings hold a sharper look on camera but do not break up as readily. Worth saying out loud: whatever is on the outside is what ends up on hands, clothes, the floor and the photographer's lens, so dark or heavily coloured finishes behave very differently from pale ones.

If you are ordering the main cake at the same time, the serving maths only applies to that one. Our guide to how much cake you need covers sizing the cake the guests actually eat, and the smash cake sits outside that calculation as an extra.

For the camera

Smash cake ideas that photograph well

The best cake smash ideas are built around how the cake will look in a frame, not how clever it is close up. A few directions worth considering.

  • Soft palettes that read on camera.Pastels, creams and single muted tones photograph beautifully against a plain backdrop and keep attention on the child. Very dark colours can be dramatic but they stain hands and clothes, and a chocolate smash cake will give you rich, messy photos and an outfit that may not recover. Plenty of parents pick a pale cake and a coloured backdrop for exactly that reason.
  • Texture instead of decoration.Ruffles, combed buttercream, rustic swirls, scalloped edges and fluffy piped finishes all catch light well and look handmade in close-up shots. They also come apart cleanly, which is the point. Texture is often the better choice for a 1st birthday cake smash because it photographs with depth and needs nothing stuck into it.
  • Simple toppers only.A soft number one, a small piped crown, a short fringe of edible flowers around the base. The topper should be something the child can knock over without a sharp edge appearing, so anything on a wire or a plastic spike generally stays off.
  • Matching the theme, or deliberately not.A smash cake can echo the colours and motifs of the main cake so the two read as a set, or it can be plain while the larger cake carries the theme. Both work. The decision is easier if you look at where the photos will be taken first.
  • Thinking about where it happens.Outdoors in an Australian summer, buttercream softens quickly and a cake will not hold a crisp finish for long in direct sun. Indoors, you control the light but you also own the mess. Tell your maker where the smash is happening and roughly what time of day, because it genuinely changes what they recommend.
One brief, two cakes

Ordering the smash cake with the main cake

Briefing both cakes in one go is almost always the better approach.

The maker buys and bakes once, works to one colour palette, and schedules both for the same day, which usually makes the pair cheaper and more consistent than two separate orders. It also avoids the awkward situation where the small cake arrives in a slightly different shade of pink from the big one.

Give your maker the date, the start time of the party, the theme or palette, the number of guests for the main cake, whether a photographer is booked, and whether you need delivery or you are picking up. Mention if the smash is happening at a studio session on a different day from the party, because that means two deliveries or two pickups and two separate timings.

Timing is the detail people forget. A smash cake is made fresh like any other cake, so it slots into the same production schedule, and popular weekends fill up well in advance. Send the brief to a few cake makers early, with both cakes described together, and compare what comes back as a package.

Say it early

Dietary needs and what to ask

If there is an allergy or a dietary requirement in the family, put it in the first message along with everything else.

It affects ingredients, equipment and scheduling, so it is not something to add on later in the process.

What any particular cake is suitable for is a conversation for you, the maker and your family's own health professional. Ask the maker directly how they handle the requirement and what they can commit to, raise anything specific with the person who looks after your child's health, and let those two answers guide the order.

In short

Bringing it together

A smash cake is a small, soft, simply decorated cake with nothing rigid inside it, ordered alongside the cake your guests will eat. Keep it low, keep the finish soft, keep the topper simple, and tell your maker where and when the smash is happening so they can build it for the conditions on the day.

Do that and the ordering is easy, which leaves you free to worry about the only genuinely difficult part: getting the outfit off afterwards. Describe both cakes in one brief, get cake maker quotes and compare what comes back.

Both cakes, one brief

Order the smash cake with the main one

One palette, one bake, one delivery. Describe both cakes together and the pair comes back cheaper and better matched than two separate orders.
